persona.name: Jonas Eriksen
persona.demographics: Raised in Lillehammer, Norway; ethnic Norwegian; lived in Oslo for university and training; currently based in Oslo but spends large blocks with national team at training bases and race venues
persona.profession: Performance Data Analyst (Cross-Country Skiing) for a national development squad
persona.education: MSc in Data Science and Sport Science, Norwegian School of Sport Sciences / University of Oslo; BSc in Statistics; certifications in Python (DataCamp), R (Tidyverse), GPS/IMU sensor analysis, and Strength & Conditioning basics
persona.socioeconomic_status: Middle Income; public sport federation role / full-time performance staff
persona.brief_background: A former junior cross-country athlete who moved into analytics after an injury, Jonas combines sensor data, power profiles, and environmental information to advise coaches on training load and race tactics. He writes scripts that automatically pull GPS/IMU and heart-rate data and produces simple visual briefs for coaches before morning meetings. Jonas will prototype a model overnight and then bike up to the stadium to test a hypothesis on snow the next morning.
persona.interests_lifestyle: cross-country skiing and backcountry touring, trail running and cycling, tinkering with sensors and open-source analysis tools, coaching a local youth ski club, reading sports physiology papers, skiing film analysis, cold-water swimming, brewing coffee, attending hackathons and sports tech meetups

general_writing_style.tone: Concise, evidence-driven and collegial: communicates findings and recommendations plainly with coaches and athletes, prioritizing actionable next steps over rhetorical flourish. Slightly informal and pragmatic — friendly but focused, acknowledges uncertainty and caveats while making clear what to try next.
general_writing_style.syntax: Predominantly short to medium-length declarative and compound sentences for clarity, with occasional complex subordinate clauses when explaining causality or method. Frequently uses imperative or checklist-style lines for recommendations and troubleshooting, and avoids long winding sentences or unnecessary qualifiers.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses sports-science and sensor vocabulary (GPS, IMU, HR, power profile, cadence, stride length, VO2max) and SI-based metrics (m/s, km/h, W/kg, bpm, kJ). Also incorporates data-engineering terms when relevant (script, pipeline, sync, raw vs filtered) and practical coaching language (lap, threshold, interval, technique).
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of acronyms and shorthand ("HR", "IMU", "CI"); moderate contractions in informal notes ("we'll", "I'll"); and pragmatic markers for quick attention: "FYI", "Heads-up", "Quick note". Typical phrases include: "FYI — model shows +2% power at 10km", "Quick check: sync timestamps and re-run the pipeline", and "Let's test this on snow tomorrow."

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: A concise briefing to the head coach before the morning meeting
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Executive, tightly focused and prioritised: start with the top-line recommendation, follow with one-sentence evidence, end with clear next steps. Sentences are short, imperative where appropriate, and avoid unnecessary qualifiers while still noting key caveats.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Use of TL;DR and direct recommendation phrases: "TL;DR: increase interval volume +5% this week"; one-line evidence snippets: "Data: mean power +2% at 10km, HR drift +3 bpm"; clear next-step imperatives: "Do: test 2x6min @ threshold tomorrow". Scenario-specific features include checklist-style lines, metric shorthand ("W/kg", "bpm", "km"), and a crisp Cause→Action sentence structure.

task_instruction: Recommend a small increase in interval volume for the development squad this week.
task_details: Squad: U23 development group (8 athletes). Recent sessions showed a slight uptick in sustainable power but mild cardiovascular drift late in long efforts. Aim: modest stimulus increase without risking overreach. Provide one-line evidence and clear next-step session to test change in tomorrow's practice.
personalized:
TL;DR: Increase interval volume +5% for the group this week to convert improved power into tolerance.
Data: mean power up +2% at 10 km efforts; HR drift +3 bpm in final 10% of long intervals; RPE unchanged.
Do: add one extra 4-min block to the planned 3x8min intervals tomorrow (target 4.0–4.2 W/kg), keep rest constant; monitor HR drift and readiness scores after session.
Caveat: stop progression if HR drift >5 bpm or RPE +2 vs baseline.

task_instruction: Advise an immediate reduction in load for an athlete showing signs of under-recovery.
task_details: Athlete: male U23, recent illness two weeks ago, returning to full training. Metrics: HRV down, resting HR elevated, poor sleep reported. Recommend a short-term plan (48–72h) and reassessment criteria for returning to normal load.
personalized:
TL;DR: Reduce load 10–15% and put athlete on active recovery for 48–72 hours. 
Data: HRV down 12% vs baseline, resting HR +5 bpm, sleep 4–5 h/night, subjective fatigue 7/10.
Do: replace two planned high-intensity sessions with low-intensity 45–60 min aerobic sessions <70% HRmax and a mobility session; recheck HRV and morning HR after 48 h and only progress if HRV recovers within 5% of baseline.
Heads-up: avoid max efforts until sleep and HRV normalise.

task_instruction: Give a concise pacing plan for the upcoming 10 km skate race based on power/terrain model.
task_details: Race: 10 km skate with two steep climbs (km 3 and km 7). Athlete sustainable power for ~35 min is 4.1 W/kg. Model predicts positive splits if athlete overpowers the first climb. Provide top-line recommendation, one-line evidence and explicit in-race targets.
personalized:
TL;DR: Hold conservative first half, then push from km 6–10; target overall negative split.
Data: model: athlete sustainable 4.1 W/kg for race duration; climbs demand short spikes to 4.6–5.0 W/kg but cause fatigue leading to +6% power loss after first climb if overpaced.
Do: instruct athlete to hold 4.0 W/kg through first 6 km (limit spikes to <15 s at 5.0 W/kg), then increase to 4.3–4.5 W/kg on final climbs; coach to cue at km 5.5 and monitor lap watts/HR.
Caveat: if HR >5 bpm above race target in first climb, drop pace and reassess.

task_instruction: Propose a short equipment trial to address a suspected suboptimal double-poling technique related to pole length.
task_details: Context: IMU and video show reduced glide and early arm drop on flat sections during max efforts. Athlete height and usual pole length specified. Recommend a one-session trial of altered pole length and objective criteria to judge success.
personalized:
TL;DR: Trial +2 cm pole length in warm-up to improve double-poling glide and force application.
Data: IMU shows decreased trunk extension and 6% lower propulsive impulse on flats during recent intervals; cadence normal but shorter effective pole plant time.
Do: test +2 cm poles during warm-up and 2x5min DP intervals at race intensity; record pole forces (if available), IMU trunk angle, and mean watts; accept change if mean propulsive impulse +4% and perceived shoulder load not increased.
FYI: revert if shoulder pain or cadence drops >5%.

task_instruction: Recommend a wax and scrape test for the stadium microclimate affecting glide on the final straight.
task_details: Issue: team observed slower speeds on final 400 m. Environment: track temp −1 to +1°C, recent solar warming midday. Provide one-line evidence from speed traces and friction estimates and a clear do-list for wax test tomorrow morning before warm-up.
personalized:
TL;DR: Run a targeted wax test on final straight with a colder base and coarser scraper pattern to regain glide. 
Data: GPS: final 400 m mean speed −4% vs same segment last week; friction estimate up ~8% from baseline; track surface variable with light solar melt patches.
Do: test three short skis tomorrow AM: current wax (control), colder base + mid-range top, and colder base + coarser scrape; run 2 flybys each and record peak speed and slip; choose fastest combination for races.
Note: bring two extra pairs for quick swaps during warm-up.

task_instruction: Alert the coach to a sensor synchronization bug and outline immediate corrective steps.
task_details: Situation: overnight pipeline flagged timing misalignment between GPS and HR streams for yesterday's intervals. Impact: interval HR and power alignment off by a few seconds, affecting threshold estimates. Provide concise evidence and direct fix steps for the analyst and coach.
personalized:
TL;DR: Fix timestamp drift before using yesterday's intervals for decisions; re-sync and re-run the pipeline now.
Data: script log shows GPS timestamps shifted +3 s vs chest HR and IMU, causing misaligned bout averaging and a ~2% error in mean interval watts.
Do: run the resync script (sync_offsets.py) with offset = −3 s, re-generate interval report, and push updated brief before morning meeting; flag any athlete with >3% change in interval power.
Quick check: if resync not possible in 20 min, exclude yesterday's interval HR-derived thresholds from today's meeting.

task_instruction: Provide a selection recommendation for the relay leg based on recent power trends.
task_details: Context: final decision on 4th leg needed. Two candidates: Athlete A (current leg) and Athlete B (reserve). Recent data: Athlete A shows performance drop in last two races; Athlete B has steady increase. Give concise top-line recommendation, one-line evidence, and the swap action.
personalized:
TL;DR: Swap Athlete A for Athlete B on the 4th leg. 
Data: Athlete A mean race watts −6% vs baseline the last two races with increased HR drift; Athlete B mean race watts +3% and better closing speed in last sessions.
Do: name Athlete B as 4th leg, notify team manager now, and brief Athlete B on pacing plan (hold 4.0 W/kg first 3 km, then push to 4.4 W/kg final 2 km); monitor athlete A in recovery plan and reassess for next event.
FYI: this reduces team risk on final climb.

task_instruction: Advise a short taper adjustment based on an overnight performance forecast model.
task_details: Model: overnight simulation predicts peak performance if high-intensity work is reduced at specific time points. Provide top-line recommendation for final 72 h, one-line model evidence, and explicit session changes for the next three days.
personalized:
TL;DR: Reduce high-intensity volume 25% over final 72 hours to maximise peak on race day. 
Data: overnight model: predicted peak performance increases ~1.8% when HI volume cut 25% at 72–24 h window; excessive HI in final 48 h shifts peak earlier.
Do: Day −3: keep planned short HI but drop one block (e.g., 3x6 min → 2x6 min); Day −2: replace HI with technique and 30–45 min easy; Day −1: short sharp activations only (4x30 s race-sharp efforts) and rest; monitor readiness and morning HR each day.
Caveat: maintain caloric intake and normal sleep hygiene to realise predicted gain.

Check strap tight and sync HR strap before tomorrow’s warm-up just to rule out any signal lag. We'll stick to 3 easy days now, then re-test 4x3 at threshold on Friday.

task_instruction: Report that 'align_gps_imu()' was pushed to dev and describe failing timestamp-drift unit test and next steps.

personalized: FYI — pushed 'align_gps_imu()' to dev (branch: dev/align-gps-imu, commit: 3f7a9b2). Quick repro: Run: python pipeline.py --date=2026-01-06 --module=sync --filter=3s. Unit tests failing: test_timestamp_drift. Symptom: timestamp drift >200 ms on device SN_42 when IMU log contains a clock rollback event. Likely cause: current align logic assumes monotonic device clocks; doesn't handle rollbacks. Immediate next steps: re-run with flag --sync-mode=hard to force alignment against GNSS time and collect debug dump by setting env DEBUG_SYNC=1. I added temporary dump to /tmp/sync_dumps/<date>/ for the failing run. Can you take the failing trace and try the hard-sync run? If that clears the test we should add a fallback branch for clock rollback and a unit test that injects a rollback event.

personalized: Quick check: added 'impute_hr_kalman()' to branch impute/kalman. Ask colleague to run simulation and compare KS-statistic.
personalized: FYI: prototype simulator added at scripts/simulate_sensors.py. Repro command: Run: python scripts/simulate_sensors.py --athlete-profile=profiles/sn42.json --duration=3600 --stride-freq-mean=0.9 --stride-freq-sd=0.05 --out=synth/sn42_1h.npz. Unit failing: test_sim_stride_freq_distribution. Symptom: generated stride freq distribution too narrow vs empirical. Fix: match empirical histogram in data/empirical/stride_freq_hist.npy by sampling via inverse CDF or increase sd dynamically per segment. task_instruction: Write a decision memo recommending adoption of a new pacing model for the development squad.
task_details: Summarize the model's main result and quantify the expected operational impact. Provide two to three clear rollout options with associated risks and a recommended next step that is time-bound. Assume the model shows a 4% improvement in pacing accuracy and that a pilot across two race venues would cost €6,000 in sensor support and personnel time.
personalized:
Summary: The new pacing model increases pacing accuracy by an estimated 4%, which we project will reduce time loss from suboptimal pacing by roughly 0.8–1.2% per race for our athletes. This translates to measurable performance gains in development-level competitions and clearer decision support for coaches.

Option A: Pilot across two venues within the next eight weeks. Implement the model for one training block and one race weekend, allocate €6,000 for sensor support and analyst time, and collect matched GPS, heart rate, and outcome data. Risk: incomplete remote-data coverage could bias results if device failures are concentrated at one venue.

Option B: Delay and expand validation to five venues over three months to increase external validity prior to any operational use. Cost increases to approximately €16,000. Risk: slower benefit delivery and missed gains during the coming competition window.

Option C: Do not adopt now and continue current decision practice while conducting passive monitoring. Cost is minimal but opportunity cost is potential performance gains lost this season.

Recommendation: Proceed with Option A. Run the pilot within the next eight weeks, with a clear data collection checklist and an on-site sensor technician assigned for each venue. Deliverables: pilot report within two weeks after the second venue and recommendation to scale or pause within four weeks of that report.

task_instruction: Request funding to purchase additional GPS+IMU units for consistent data collection.
task_details: Explain the operational need, quantified improvement in data completeness and decision quality, three procurement options (buy, lease, or delay), estimated costs and implementation timeline, and risks. Assume buying 20 units costs €40,000, leasing for a season is €12,000, and delayed purchase risks further data gaps.
personalized:
Summary: Procuring 20 additional GPS+IMU units will increase usable athlete-session coverage from approximately 62% to 92%, improving the reliability of load and technique assessments and enabling consistent model inputs for the squad.

Option A: Purchase 20 units at a one-time cost of €40,000 and maintain them internally. This provides long-term availability and lower per-season cost but requires storage, maintenance, and minor staff time for calibration. Risk: upfront capital outlay and potential device obsolescence over multiple seasons.

Option B: Lease equivalent units for the season at €12,000. This reduces initial expenditure and includes maintenance, but limits availability in concurrent events and increases recurring cost if used long-term. Risk: potential scheduling conflicts during overlapping events.

Option C: Delay procurement and continue with current inventory. Short-term cost saving but continued data gaps that impair model validation and coaching decisions. Risk: biased analytics and missed opportunities for objective load management.

Recommendation: Approve leasing for the upcoming season (Option B) to cover the immediate competition window while we confirm integration and maintenance processes. Prepare a purchase proposal for next budget cycle contingent on demonstrated return from the leased units. Timeline: lease agreement within three weeks and deployment before the next competition block.

task_instruction: Propose hiring a short-term data engineer to stabilise the data pipeline.
task_details: State the pipeline issue, quantify impact on report delivery and coaching decisions, present hiring options (contractor for 3 months, internal reallocation, or deprioritise), estimated costs (contractor €18,000), and risks. Recommend a time-bound hire if appropriate.
personalized:
Summary: Current pipeline instability causes an average two-day delay in morning brief production for coaches, reducing the utility of our model outputs for race-day planning. Stabilising the pipeline will restore same-morning brief delivery and improve tactical decisions.

Option A: Hire a contract data engineer for three months at an estimated cost of €18,000 to implement robust ingestion, automated checks, and alerting. This is the fastest route to restore reliable delivery. Risk: contractor onboarding time and reliance on an external resource for knowledge transfer.

Option B: Reallocate existing staff for a temporary fix. This avoids extra cost but will reduce analyst capacity for athlete support and model refinement, with a risk of incomplete remediation.

Option C: Deprioritise pipeline work and accept delayed briefs. Short-term cost saving but continued reduction in decision quality. Risk: impaired coach trust in analytics and missed race-performance opportunities.

Recommendation: Proceed with Option A to hire a contractor immediately. Contract start within two weeks and delivery of automated checks and alerting within six weeks. Ensure knowledge transfer sessions are scheduled in the final two weeks of the contract.

task_instruction: Recommend a validation study of the model across altitude and temperature ranges.
task_details: Summarise why validation is needed, expected variance in model performance (assume ±3% across conditions), present two study designs (controlled lab plus field sampling vs expanded field-only sampling), costs and timelines, and risks. Provide a recommended design and time-bound milestone.
personalized:
Summary: Preliminary results indicate the model performs consistently in moderate conditions but may vary by up to ±3% across high-altitude or very cold venues. Validation across these ranges is necessary to ensure reliable operational guidance.

Option A: Run a mixed validation with controlled lab sessions to simulate physiological stress and field sampling at three representative venues. Estimated cost €10,000 and timeline eight weeks. This provides causal insight and field confirmation. Risk: higher cost and logistical complexity.

Option B: Conduct expanded field-only sampling across five venues during the season at an estimated cost of €6,500 and timeline 10–12 weeks. This offers broader ecological validity but less control over confounders. Risk: environmental variability may obscure causal drivers of model variance.

Option C: Accept current validation levels and apply blanket model adjustments. Low cost but high risk of miscalibration at extreme venues.

Recommendation: Approve Option A. Begin lab sessions and schedule field visits over the next eight weeks. Deliver a validation report with condition-specific adjustment factors within three weeks of completing field sampling.

task_instruction: Draft a contingency plan for sensor failure during competitions.

Option A: Carry two calibrated spare devices per event and assign an on-site technician. Estimated incremental cost €1,500 per event for spares and logistics. This provides immediate replacement capability. Risk: marginal increase in packing and handling tasks.

Option B: Train staff to perform structured manual observation protocols when device data are unavailable. Low cost but less precise inputs for the analytics pipeline. Risk: reduced objectivity and potential reporting inconsistency.

Option C: Withdraw analytics support when device failure occurs. Minimal cost but high operational risk and lost decision support. Risk: coaches make uninformed choices during critical periods.

Recommendation: Approve Option A for the upcoming competition window and implement Option B as a fallback. Procure spares and confirm technician assignments within two weeks before the next event.

task_instruction: Propose a rapid-iteration plan to prototype overnight model updates and test on snow the next morning at a trial venue.
task_details: Describe how the rapid loop operates, quantify expected iteration speed gains (e.g., reduce model-to-test cycle from two weeks to 24 hours), list options for scaling the process (ad-hoc testing, scheduled early-morning tests, or formal lab replication), costs and risks. personalized:
Summary: Establishing a rapid-iteration protocol where model prototypes are run overnight and hypotheses are tested on snow the following morning will reduce the model-to-test cycle from roughly two weeks to 24 hours, accelerating evidence-based adjustments.

Option A: Ad-hoc overnight prototypes followed by immediate morning field tests when staff and athletes are available. This is flexible and low cost but relies on chance alignment of personnel and venue conditions. Risk: inconsistent coverage and limited replicability.

Option B: Schedule regular early-morning test windows twice per week at a designated training site and assign a rotating analyst-coach pair. This formalises the process, ensures availability, and enables systematic recording. Risk: small recurring staff time commitment.

Option C: Attempt full lab replication before snow testing. This increases control but substantially slows the loop and reduces ecological validity. Risk: loss of real-world relevance.

Recommendation: Implement Option B. Start twice-weekly early-morning test windows at the stadium within the next week. Assign a rotating analyst-coach pair and require a one-page test report within 24 hours. Review the process after four scheduled tests and evaluate scale-up.

task_instruction: Provide a couple of short, fun at-home drills parents can do with their child during a busy week.
task_details: Give two simple, game-based drills (balance and short intervals) that take under 20 minutes, explain purpose in plain language, suggest frequency (e.g., two times this week), and include a supportive phrasing for parents to encourage kids.
personalized: Quick idea for busy weeks: two short, fun drills you can do at home. First, balance hop: mark a short line and have the child hop across and back on one foot, then the other; five hops each side helps balance and ankle strength. Second, speed play: ten bursts of 15 seconds brisk running or fast skiing-in-place with 45 seconds easy walking between; this keeps legs sharp without tiring them. Do either drill twice this week for 10–15 minutes each time. Make it a game and cheer them on — kids respond best to fun. Cheers, Jonas

task_instruction: Request loan of prototype carbon poles for on-snow validation.
task_details: Ask sponsor for three prototype carbon poles with reduced shaft mass and modified flex pattern. Specify primary and secondary metrics: mass reduction in grams and impact on skier power output and sprint split times. Include shipping address (team base in Oslo), contact for coordination, and request for any technical spec sheets and recommended stiffness selection.
personalized: Hello — quick request from the national development squad. Request: loan three prototype carbon poles with the reduced-mass shaft and the stiffer tip/flex variant for a 6-week validation. Primary metric: mass reduction in g and delta W/kg at 10–30 s sprint efforts. Secondary metrics: 1 km and 5 km sprint split times and subjective handling on corners. Timeline: delivery by Week 1, on-snow test window Weeks 2–4, return by end of Week 6. Ship to the team base in Oslo; I can provide the precise address and athlete pairing once you confirm availability. Please include recommended stiffness selection and any tech sheets. If available, confirm shipping ETA and who I should cc for logistics. Thanks — Jonas (performance data analyst), cell +47 9xx xxx xx.

Send tech sheets and recommended binding set-up. I’ll coordinate receiving with our Oslo base; confirm availability and shipping ETA. Cheers, Jonas.

task_instruction: Report an acute training-load spike and recommend immediate recovery actions.
task_details: Athlete: U23 male skier. Last 7 days training load (session-RPE): 1,150 AU; previous 28-day mean: 650 AU. Acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) = 1.77. HRV trend down 8% vs baseline. No reported injury, increased perceived muscle soreness. Request: concise clinical note to S&C/physio with suggested immediate interventions and simple tests to check readiness.
personalized:
Subject: Acute load spike — immediate recovery recommendation

FYI — Marius U23 shows a clear acute load spike last week. 7-day load = 1,150 AU; 28-day mean = 650 AU; ACWR = 1.77. HRV down ~8% from his 4-week baseline and subjective soreness up. No acute injury reported, but ACWR >1.5 puts him in the high-risk band for soft-tissue overload.

Recommend immediate steps: reduce total volume by ~40% for 3–5 days, keep low-impact aerobic recovery (easy ski/bike) and avoid high-intensity intervals. Prioritise sleep and nutrition, and add two passive recovery modalities this week (contrast bath or massage) if available.

Propose quick tests to guide progression: orthostatic HR test in the morning, single-leg CMJ (force plate or contact mat) to check neuromuscular readiness, and a 60s submax ski erg at low intensity to monitor HR response. If CMJ power is down >10% or orthostatic HR rises >10 bpm, continue low-load recovery another 3–5 days.

Can you run the CMJ and orthostatic test tomorrow morning and share results? I’ll hold high-intensity sessions until we confirm readiness.

task_instruction: Flag a persistent left/right force asymmetry and propose targeted S&C and clinical tests.
task_details: Athlete: Development squad female skier. IMU and force-plate derived single-leg force show left/right peak force asymmetry of 9.5% across repeated trials during bounding drills. Ground contact time asymmetry 11%. No acute pain but coach reports reduced left-side push-off. Suggest S&C interventions and clinical tests (isometric mid-thigh pull, 2D video of stride, single-leg hop). Invite physiotherapist to assess possible underlying issue.
personalized:
Subject: Left/right force asymmetry >9% — S&C/physio input requested

Quick note — sensor data from last three sessions show consistent left/right peak force asymmetry = 9.5% and ground contact time asymmetry = 11% during bounding and high-speed drills. Athlete reports no sharp pain but describes weaker left push-off on steeper pitches.

Implications: asymmetry >8% is linked with higher re-injury and performance loss in sprint/propulsive tasks. Worth treating as a bilateral deficit rather than normal variation.

Propose immediate checks and interventions: clinical screen for hip/glute activation and ankle stiffness, 2D frontal/sagittal video of running/striding to assess frontal-plane compensation, and isometric mid-thigh pull to get maximal unilateral force numbers. Start unilateral S&C emphasis: split squats, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, and unilateral loaded hops with reduced volume but higher intent.

Can you run the clinical screen and 2D stride video this week? I’ll schedule an isometric mid-thigh pull in the lab and share raw force curves so we can set unilateral targets. If pain or ROM deficits appear, we’ll pause plyometrics and focus on corrective therapy.

task_instruction: Provide a pre-competition taper recommendation balancing volume and neuromuscular potency.
task_details: Athlete: National-level male with two key races in 10 days. Recent training load high; CMJ and sprint metrics show slight drop (≈6%). Goal: preserve neuromuscular power while reducing fatigue. personalized:
Subject: Taper plan for two races in 10 days — preserve power, reduce fatigue

Quick plan for the next 10 days: reduce weekly training volume by ~40% overall but keep intensity exposure. Maintain two short high-intensity sessions at race pace (one 3×3min at race intent on day −7 and one 2×2min at race intent on day −3). Keep sessions brief and with full recovery between reps.

S&C guidance: drop total strength volume by ~50% but keep neuromuscular potency with two activation sessions focusing on low-volume, high-intent lifts (2–3 sets of 2–3 reps at >85% intent) and one short plyometric activation 48 hours before races (6–8 explosive reps). Avoid heavy eccentric loads in the final 7 days.

Monitoring and criteria: retest CMJ 48 hours pre-first race; if CMJ power is within 5% of baseline proceed. If CMJ still down >8%, reduce pre-race intensity and add extra passive recovery.

Can you adjust the S&C calendar accordingly and run the CMJ 48 hours pre-race? I’ll coordinate on exact session content and share the power targets.

task_instruction: Log results of overnight model prediction tested on-snow with a 10 km time trial.
task_details: Record timestamp, environmental conditions, devices and sampling rates, model prediction (power % change at 10 km), measured power and time, short reproducible processing notes (filters/sync), and immediate next steps to adjust model bias.
personalized:
2026-01-06 07:05 — 10 km TT test vs overnight model
Temp=-6°C; wind calm; snow packed groomed
Athlete mass=74.8 kg; skis=set A (HF base); wax=klister-lite
Devices: GPS@10Hz (Garmin), IMU@200Hz (Xsens), HR strap (Polar), pole-force sensor prototype
Model_pred: +2.0% mean power @10km (trained on slope-seg features)
Raw processing: Filter=3s low-pass position; sync_offset(GPS↔IMU)=+0.5s; pole-force→power algo v0.9
Obs: Measured mean power +1.8% at 10km (close); TT time +4 s slower than predicted; bias ≈ -0.2% vs model
Detail: Surge segments on climbs show model overpredicts by ~4% (short, high-intensity bursts)
Next: Apply additive bias correction -0.2% to baseline; retrain model with extra climb-burst samples; test again on similar course within 48h
Note: Save raw files to /data/2026-01-06/TT01 and mark as validation set

2026-01-08 09:00 — GPS corner jitter check during mixed lap
Temp -2°C; track wet; course includes two tight corners at km 1.2 and 3.7
Device: Garmin GPS@10Hz; IMU@200Hz used for ground-truth heading
Problem: GPS position jitter visible on corners → inflated instantaneous speed and false accelerations
Processing tests: Filter window=3s → speed variance reduced 28% but preserves accelerations on exits; Filter window=5s → variance reduced 48% but smoothed legitimate accelerations
Metric: median corner speed error (vs IMU-derived) = 0.9 km/h (no filter), 0.6 km/h (3s), 0.35 km/h (5s)
Trade-off: 3s keeps short surges; 5s over-smooths tactical pushes
Decision: set Filter=4s for pipeline as compromise; document per-segment override possible for interval analysis
Next: rerun batch for last two weeks with Filter=4s and compare lap-split consistency

Session: steady 40min with 6x30s strides; temp -7°C

Method: cross-correlation between IMU pole-strike envelope and HR rise on strides; confirm with GPS speed peaks

Action: update metadata header with offsets; set auto-calc routine to compute cross-corr on first 10min of each session and store offset in manifest
Next: implement threshold check: if |offset|>1.0s flag for manual review

general_writing_style.syntax: Predominantly short to medium-length declarative and compound sentences for clarity, with occasional complex subordinate clauses when explaining causality or method. Frequently uses imperative or checklist-style lines for recommendations and troubleshooting, and avoids long winding sentences or unnecessary qualifiers.
general_writing_style.lexicon: Uses sports-science and sensor vocabulary (GPS, IMU, HR, power profile, cadence, stride length, VO2max) and SI-based metrics (m/s, km/h, W/kg, bpm, kJ). Also incorporates data-engineering terms when relevant (script, pipeline, sync, raw vs filtered) and practical coaching language (lap, threshold, interval, technique).
general_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of acronyms and shorthand ("HR", "IMU", "CI"); moderate contractions in informal notes ("we'll", "I'll"); and pragmatic markers for quick attention: "FYI", "Heads-up", "Quick note". Typical phrases include: "FYI — model shows +2% power at 10km", "Quick check: sync timestamps and re-run the pipeline", and "Let's test this on snow tomorrow."

contextual_writing_style.scenario_description: A personal field notebook or lab-journal entry after an experiment or test run
contextual_writing_style.detailed_style: Terse, timestamped and reproducibility-focused: short log entries with clear metadata (time, conditions), bullet-equivalent plain lines for observations and immediate next steps. Use of abbreviations and parameter values is standard; the tone is functional and archival.
contextual_writing_style.linguistic_patterns: Log-entry format examples: "2026-01-06 06:30 — test run, -5°C, ski set A"; observation/action shorthand: "Obs: GPS jitter @ corners; Next: apply filter window=3s"; parameterized notes: "Filter=3s; sync_offset=+0.5s; cadence target=85 rpm". Scenario-specific features include timestamps, compact parameter notation, and imperative next-step lines for reproducibility.

task_instruction: Log a short race-tactics simulation test during a pursuit rehearsal, comparing predicted and actual energetic cost of a mid-race surge.
task_details: Include timestamp, athlete mass, simulation parameters (baseline pacing, surge magnitude and duration), observed surge timing and extra energy cost in kJ, and next simulation adjustments to match field data.
personalized:
2026-01-15 10:05 — pursuit surge sim vs field
Athlete mass=75 kg; baseline pacing simulated from model (steady 4.2 W/kg)
Planned surge: +0.15 W/kg for 20s at km 6 (model predicted extra cost 6.4 kJ)
Field: athlete surged at km 6.2 for 22s; measured additional cost (pole-force power integration) = 8.1 kJ
Discrepancy: model underestimates surge cost by ~27%
Cause hypothesis: model underrepresents anaerobic/acceleration inefficiency during rapid power ramps; current model assumes linear metabolic cost
Action: incorporate transient cost multiplier for power ramps >0.1 W/kg/s; initial multiplier=1.25 applied reduces predicted error to <5%
Next: run 5 simulated surges with multiplier and validate on two athletes in next session; document multiplier as transient_cost_coeff=1.25 (provisional)
